utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. McCloskey: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I want to show you a short clip this morning to see if you can identify the kinds of vehicles that you were driving that day in Konjevic Polje. So that should come up on your screen, but as we're waiting for that, let me ask you: Were there any prisoners taken back to the Bratunac Brigade military police that day that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can have a specification from where. From where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We know where he is, Your Honour. This is cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. Well, I believe that Mr. McCloskey will rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Bratunac Brigade prisoners taken to the military police on the day that you were in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know that there were prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember one prisoner named Senad Senadovic or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling us earlier about Momir Nikolic getting a couple of prisoners there at Konjevic Polje and taking them back to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that from Konjevic Polje he took one person. That's what I heard. I did not see that. And that that person is Senad Residovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. What do you know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction Resid Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said that I think he took this person from Konjevic Polje and we stayed in Konjevic Polje during that time; whereas, he took that person to Bratunac and then went back there. So there were no other persons. I don't know of any other persons, so I know of this one person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Momir Nikolic with this prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who did you hear about it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he took someone. When he came back, he said that he took someone who had worked in the MUP earlier on and then -- I mean, I didn't know these people. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that prisoner when you went back to the MP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a gaol at the MP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the military police was just one room where persons who evaded going to the front line were kept. It was not a classical prison. It was just a room, a regular room. It wasn't a classical prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a place there where you kept Muslim prisoners at this time frame?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- we'll show you this video, hope it comes up on your screen, see if you recognise the vehicle that should be in this screen. And I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that vehicle in the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the kind of vehicle you were driving that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could freeze that. Where were you driving the vehicle from? Can you see the driver's seat in this picture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot orient myself properly. I know that the driver's seat is on the left-hand side, and up on the top there is a turret so you can close it. Now, whether it's this -- I mean, I know there is this seat, there is this turret where there is a driver's seat. There is this command seat, if I can call it that, where the commander sits or the signalman, I don't know who, and this other machine gun, this weapon, you see, on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. When you were driving the vehicle, did you have your head sticking out the top of the vehicle or were you inside it when it was being driven that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what time that day did you end up going back to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, from where I went to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You were in Konjevic Polje. Did you go back to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was in the afternoon. I don't know what time it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any Muslims along the road when you drove back from Konjevic Polje to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw -- well, first right out of Konjevic Polje there was a column, two by two, they were walking towards Konjevic Polje. Perhaps there were five or ten soldiers, I did not know. Youngish soldiers, say around 20, 25 years old. And just before Kravica on the left-hand side, there were perhaps 50 to 100 persons who were sitting, who were sitting on the ground close to one another. And there were some soldiers by them and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these Muslim men sitting on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know. I don't know, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the men you saw walking towards Konjevic Polje, were those Muslims or were those Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb soldiers, I said that there were perhaps only about 10 Serb soldiers, and the column was about 50 metres long. They were walking two by two in this column in the direction of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there Muslims walking in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were Muslims. And the soldiers were armed, whereas these other men were not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether these were Ministry of Interior soldiers or army soldiers that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He says Ministry of Interior soldiers. Now we've gone from MUP soldiers to a creative way of referring to them as soldiers by saying Ministry of Interior soldiers. They're not soldiers. They're police, they're special police. They may be armed like soldiers, but they're police and I would like some specificity here. Otherwise we're going to have a mess at the end of the trial, Your Honour, so please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We come across the same issue as always, to distinguish between the police and the soldiers. I think the last time we used the term "man."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to argue over this. Men with guns and armaments are soldiers. And I've made very clear that they Ministry of Interior. I'm not trying to suggest that these guys are army, so I don't know what the gripe is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well. Let's find a middle way, and that is man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you have any idea what unit these armed men were that were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What unit do you think they were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know. I didn't know then. And it's not that I could look at them and see whether they had insignia or not. I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. About what time did you get back to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that we returned sometime in the afternoon. I can't say exactly what time it was, but I know it was afternoon. I don't know exactly. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go when you got there, to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At headquarters, I left the APC there and I went to the military police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do for the rest of the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember what I did exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what any of your -- what any of the Bratunac Brigade military police officers were doing that afternoon, that evening, when you were back at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were very few members of the unit there and they were all scattered around. The officers securing Fontana and the school where the members of UNPROFOR were, or rather, the Dutch Battalion, then security of the command post of the brigade headquarters, duty of the military police, and then of course bringing into custody persons who were fleeing from their units, who were engaged in looting, well that's what the police did. Now, what every person did specifically is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there Bratunac Brigade military police officers in Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If General Mladic was there, then they were there. If he was not up there, then no members of the military police were supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why your military policeman Radenko Zaric would have told the OTP that he was in Potocari on those days with -- on orders from you to secure the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. I don't mean to object. I assume that the Prosecution has a good faith basis. I would prefer to do it the classical way, and that is to show the gentleman the exact language of what Mr. Radenko Zaric has said, give him an opportunity to look at it, and then give a proper response, just to make sure the Prosecution is not misquoting from the statement. And I'm not suggesting that he is, but just so we have a clear record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what is the traditional way, but in these proceedings, it's allowed that the counsel put questions to this witness first to see his response. If the witness did not remember anything about this matter, the counsel could show him the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I assume, however, for our benefit, for our benefit, that we will be getting some kind of a line, page, so we could check it, as opposed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends. We have to save time. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why Radenko Zaric would say that he received orders from you to go to Potocari on those days to secure the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he said that. I don't know that I sent him to do that, to secure the Muslims, because it was not the task of the military police to secure Muslims right there at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why Radenko Zaric would say that he was there with about 20 other Bratunac Brigade military policemen to do that very task on your orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a military police platoon has about 30 men, then you can see for yourself that it is impossible in addition to all other duties involved to have some 20 military policemen be assigned to secure Muslims in Potocari. Ten men stay at the command post to secure the officers of the higher command of the Main Staff and so on and so forth and then for security at the hospital where the Muslim wounded were, the sick. Then also at the high school in Bratunac, the security there. So I cannot understand, how can these 30 men be assigned to all these different places. If that is possible, congratulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't say 30, he said about 20. Momir Nikolic said about 10. And you're saying that there was no one there, except those that were securing General Mladic. Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I know that I did not send anyone to guard the Muslims, to secure the Muslims, nor was this among the tasks to secure Muslims in Potocari. It was officers in Potocari who were supposed to be secured, that is to say those who were up there, General Mladic and I don't know who else had asked that. But it was security in terms of their own persons that was needed. The Muslims didn't have to be secured. The Dutch Battalion was there, the entire Dutch Battalion that was there with its vehicles, and it was not necessary for the military police to secure them there when UNPROFOR was there -- rather, the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Muslims didn't need any security there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, that mischaracterises the statement. That's not exactly what the gentleman indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It certainly is, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we are going to hear what the witness is going to indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are going to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is pure obstructionism, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that the Muslims didn't need any security those days. The Dutch handled it all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I'm saying in Potocari itself, in Potocari itself -- I mean, I did not remember that there was any military police there. Perhaps somebody else told them to go there to secure something, but I did not order anyone to give security for them and I could not have done this on my own. Nobody had issued me such orders. Nobody had ordered me to do that, to provide security for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing the video clip or the still photo of Radenko Zaric in Potocari by the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was supposed to provide security for General Mladic, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the evening of the 13th, were there any Muslim men detained in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that one evening they brought them from somewhere, but I don't know whether it was the 13th. They were in schools. But now whether it was the 13th, I really cannot remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What schools were the Muslim men in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that now as well, when I came here, and I said so in Banja Luka, too, I showed on the aerial image of Bratunac where these facilities were. It is the former elementary school Vuk Karadzic. Nowadays this school is called Branko Radicevic. Then old school for civil engineering, which is also near that school, then the hangar, and I don't know about other places. Well, they were probably in vehicles, because there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I've got a copy of what you helped us with in Banja Luka. It's Exhibit P-167, and if we could give that to the witness and if we can put parts of it on the ELMO that will show some of the various schools. Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, on this exhibit, are there any names on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's been properly looked after by Ms. Stewart, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could just take a while to orient yourself to that photo. You can look directly at the photo, Mr. Witness, but if it could stay on the ELMO, though -- well, yeah, let him look at it first and then if we could put it on the ELMO. And can you point to the area where the Muslim men were staying. And you can orient that any way you like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do it in the right order. This is letter A, as far as I can see. This is where the brigade headquarters was. The letter B is the facility where the military police was. This is where the elementary school was, the former elementary school, Vuk Karadzic, now called Branko Radicevic this is the facility that is called the hangar and this is the old civil engineering school that I already referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, what letter did you mark those three schools with for those three buildings? Is that an H?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: H, H is the hangar. G is the elementary school, if I can see properly the letter G. And the letter I denotes the old civil engineering school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were the Muslim men being held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, here, within this circle. The elementary school, the hangar, and the old civil engineering school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you just tell us what else you've marked as you were going through and tell us what letters. After the schools, what else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter D denotes the city stadium in Bratunac right over here. Then over here, the letter F, this is the high school, the high school centre where the members of the Dutch Battalion were. That was also secured by the military police. And over here under the letter E is where the elementary school is. Hadzimidhat used to be its name and now it's called Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody staying in letter E?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one was staying in letter E in this school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any Bratunac Brigade military police securing prisoners in the three schools you've mentioned, G, H, and I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe during the one night that they were detained here, there were people securing the facility. I'm not sure who. Very few military policemen, I'm not sure if they had any vehicles. I didn't want to go there and I couldn't go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to your knowledge, were Bratunac Brigade military policemen securing the prisoners in any of those schools, G, H, and I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. They were providing security somewhere. Whether in vehicles driving around or in one of the schools, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many military police officers from Bratunac were providing security for prisoners in those schools?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to those schools during the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Maybe I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you go to those schools in the evening to inspect troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for me to go there. What was I supposed to be doing there? I didn't feel like going; it's as simple as that. I didn't want to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing in the evening the day before you went up to Zvornik with the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the military police building. I was doing nothing in particular. There was nothing in particular for me to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we're through with that exhibit. And just to clarify, you filled out this exhibit in Banja Luka during your interview in Banja Luka. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall telling the OTP that military police were guarding prisoners at those schools during your Banja Luka interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the same thing that I've just told you now. I told you they were providing security, but I didn't know how many military policemen were there. However, not a sufficient number to provide security for three different buildings with 100 metres' distance between each. And there were vehicles there, as I was later to find out, full of men -- full of detainees. So the military police were in no position to provide security for all of those. There were too few of them. I'm not sure about the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey indicated, he said: "What were you doing in the evening the day before you went up to Zvornik with the convoy?" There has been no testimony about Zvornik. I was wondering whether he misspoke. Is this about Konjevic Polje or is it testimony to come? Because we do know that he went to Zvornik at one point, but I don't believe there has been testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas. If I remember correctly, the witness said so yesterday, one day he was going to Konjevic Polje and the other day he was with a convoy to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This evening we're talking about, did the Bratunac Brigade military police have assistance from others in securing or guarding all the Muslims that were in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was another unit there providing security. The military police were assisting them. They were not the ones assisting the military police. It was the other way around. The military police were helping them to provide security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that they were assisting each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Something like that. It was the same assignment for both of the units. They were guarding the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who issued that assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear him issue that assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He said that that was supposed to be secured, that was to be secured because it was a village and there were very few capable or able-bodied men back in town. A lot of Muslim prisoners were being brought in to the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did Momir Nikolic issue that assignment to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was present when he issued that assignment to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who else was present. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the other unit that was taking part in the securing of these prisoners, besides the Bratunac Brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this other unit was. I'm not sure if it was from the Bratunac Brigade at all. There was another unit there, it's just that I'm not sure which one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any coordination with that unit yourself so that you could assist each other in the best way possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you give anyone in the Bratunac Brigade orders based on Mr. Nikolic's orders to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood your question. I'm sorry, what do you mean, did I give any orders?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when Nikolic ordered -- you just said that Nikolic ordered you to use Bratunac Brigade military police to secure the Muslims. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you issue orders to Bratunac Brigade military police to secure those premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did. I don't know. I can't remember, but I must have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you receive reports from the military police that were securing those Muslim prisoners that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive reports from the Bratunac Brigade military police that were securing those Muslims the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I received any reports. I know that the night they were securing them, I received orders to leave. I didn't even know where I was going. They told me to take a car and to park at the junction near the bus stop. And the people from the military police and the people who were in the school, I didn't see any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you to take a car and go to a bus stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vujadin Popovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did he do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was about 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's the following day. I'll get to there in a minute. Did you receive any reports that there were bodies of Muslims around the schools?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any talk of bodies, Muslim bodies, around Bratunac from that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about that, but later on. I heard people talk. After I returned from Zvornik, maybe five or six days later was the first time I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you heard about bodies in Bratunac from that time period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that during the night those who were staying in vehicles or in schools had revolted and made an attempt to flee. I heard that some of the members from those units that were there fired shots after them, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's how the bodies were created, rioting Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's what he heard. He's not stating that's what happened. He's stating that's what he heard from other -- it's hearsay. It's very clear. Now he's trying to demean the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not trying to demean the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think you made a comment. Not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was meant to be a question. I'll make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying the stories of the bodies are from rioting Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any accounts that Serbs were outside buses and trucks and calls for Muslims from particular villages and taking them off the trucks and killing them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next morning. Can you tell us what your first assignment was that next morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first assignment was to start up the APC and park it near the bus stop. There's a junction there. One road forks off towards the school, or rather, the schools -- the street is perhaps between 300 and 400 metres long. I stopped there. I didn't know what I was to do next. I didn't know where I would be sent to. I was just told to get there. And once I was there, Colonel Popovic left and came back and told me to turn the vehicle around to face Kravica and Konjevic Polje. I turned the vehicle around and he told me to stay put, so I did for a while. He came again and told me to move as far as the distribution building where the road turned off to go to the headquarters. I moved the building [as interpreted] as far as the turnoff point, and the military vehicle arrived. They asked me whether I needed fuel. A cisterna had arrived, a military cisterna. I knew nothing about the vehicle. I didn't even know what its capacity was for fuel, the capacity of its tank. The man spoke to me and said Colonel Popovic told you to get some fuel, so I did. I got two full tanks of fuel, and I kept on waiting. Shall I continue my story or do you want to ask any questions at this point?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you can just continue your story. Tell us who's with you and what you do may be the simplest way to get through it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikola Popovic and Mile Petrovic were with me near the vehicle. I was standing there for some time at the junction near the bus stop. I can't remember exactly how long. I can't remember how long I was standing there at the gate near the headquarters. Colonel Popovic came along again with a vehicle and he told me to move further down the road and to follow him. So I followed him for about a kilometre in the direction of Konjevic Polje. And I stopped in the village of Repovac. On the way out from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, there is a Vihor transport company parking lot there to the right. I passed the parking lot and stopped the vehicle. I was there. I remember it was very hot. I stayed there until half past 1.00 or perhaps 2.00. That's how long I waited before I turned around and saw a column forming behind me. A column of buses and lorries with people in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What people were in them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the Muslims who had been staying in those schools.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any women in that group on the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I saw. I only saw the first vehicle behind me, but there must have been many more. I couldn't even see the end of the column. There's a sharp turn to the left on the road to Bratunac, so I could see as far as the curve. But I didn't see the rest of the column. My assumption was that it must have been quite long, since I was told to move ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another vehicle arrived. I don't know whether anyone else was there with Colonel Popovic. The navy blue Golf vehicle appeared and parked in front of me. And I was told to follow the vehicle. So I set out, followed the car, and the convoy set out behind me following me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Momir Nikolic at any time that morning before you set off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him. I probably did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived at the junction in Konjevic Polje. The Golf turned right, and I followed it in the direction of Zvornik. We passed through the town of Zvornik and reached a neighbourhood called Karakaj or rather a village called Karakaj where there was another junction to the left --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the Zvornik Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We didn't stop anywhere along the way. We just kept on driving. As far as the junction in Karakaj, there's a sign, a road sign saying Sapna. I was convinced that those persons were being taken, because that's what had been agreed at the headquarters, and Nikolic said so, that these persons would be exchanged. He said, do you know how many Serbs had to stay behind in Tuzla. I lived in Tuzla and I was aware of how many Serbs there still were. He said that those persons were to be exchanged which only seemed logical to me. So we drove towards Sapna, at that time under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that headquarters, that Momir Nikolic said this in relation to the trip you were taking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was being said that or he may have said it the previous day. As soon as they got to Bratunac, they would be sent on to Muslim territory, same as the women and children. No one was talking about liquidation or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Momir Nikolic before this had said that these Muslims are going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He said they would be. And everyone was saying that, even Mladic himself, General Mladic, said that the first to be taken away would be the women and children, due to excessive heat. And then the men would follow after them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about what happened to the Muslim men the day before your trip to Zvornik at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to hear that some 500 to 1.000 men were butchered at the Kravica warehouse on the evening of the 13th of July? They weren't exchanged. You never heard about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard about that. I did hear in Bijeljina, or rather, in Banja Luka. I heard later, once the war was over. But until then, I hadn't known anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where do you go leading this convoy of Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once we turned off to go to Sapna -- I wasn't familiar with the area because I had never taken the road before. We drove there. We turned off right. It was a comparatively narrow road. There was an asphalt bridge that was so narrow I could hardly cross it. It's a wide, large vehicle, so the bridge was hardly wide enough for me to cross and the other vehicles followed. We reached a school to the right of the road, and we stopped there. There were perhaps about ten soldiers there. We stopped there. I turned the vehicle around, and I saw the school in front of me. The unloading of men from the vehicles following me began. I saw that there was enough space for me to drive through, so I just set off and drove straight back. Colonel Popovic was asking me to stay there, but I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many vehicles of Muslims got unloaded while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps between five and ten vehicles. I'm not sure about the number, but there may have been between five and ten vehicles being unloaded. There were tow trucks there. There were buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many Muslims could fit in a bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove a bus and I knew that you could fit -- well, when those vehicles were coming, no one -- I could see that no one was standing in the buses. Everyone was seated. And I knew that you could fit between 40 and 50 people into a bus. Now as for a tow trucks, I'm not sure because they were covered with tarp, and I didn't know how many people were in there. I didn't count them on their way out. They would just pass by and go straight into the building there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what orders did you receive once you were at this school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive any orders there. Popovic, Colonel Popovic, went there, and I was just standing there. I couldn't go back. I had no where to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I waited there until there was enough space for me to drive through and back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just left without any orders from anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have any orders when you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Popovic told me to stay right there, but I said that I had to go back, because Nikolic had told me to drive straight back, that I would be needed at the headquarters, so I drove right back. I didn't feel like staying there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Nikolic tell you that? You just told us you didn't see Nikolic that morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I didn't see Nikolic. I said I might have seen him but I couldn't remember. That's what I said. Secondly, this may have just been an excuse for me to drive back as soon as possible because I didn't feel like staying, as simple as that. And I thought that we were near the Muslim-held -- Muslim-controlled territory, and I thought the rest of the crowd who were there could just go on and go on with the exchanges and I wouldn't be needed there. So I just drove back to my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses and trucks did you pass when you turned around and drove back to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many more. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the column split up and went in other directions from where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long exactly the column was. I know what I saw when I was at the head of the column and while I was driving. I was looking in my rear-view mirror and I can only tell you about what I saw in my rear-view mirror, how long the column was. But it didn't seem to split up or go in any other direction while I was driving. But I didn't stop on the way, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other Bratunac Brigade military police, aside from you and the two people you've mentioned assigned to this convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I knew of. I didn't know that they were there at all providing any kind of escort for the convoy, but I certainly assigned no one. I was ordered to be there. I didn't know where we were headed. I didn't know why I found myself at the junction. I knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember me showing you some pictures of schools in my office on Sunday? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to recognise one of those pictures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised the school where we had come, where these Muslims were taken off the vehicles and then I went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we'll put the picture of a school up on your screen. That is Exhibit P-13.4. Is that the school that you recall going to that day where the Muslims were dropped off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in Banja Luka, this photograph was not there. If you remember, this is how I described it, as a matter of fact, that this is what the school looked like. I was standing right over here from where this photograph was actually taken, because I turned around here and then went back with the vehicle here. But this is exactly where I was, from where the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if we could go back to the military police log briefly, which I'll have an Exhibit number in one second. It is 92. And I know you've seen this. Perhaps I can just read you the entry that says 14/15 July. It says: "The police was engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees." Do you recall reading that log entry in my office? You can see it if you'd like. It's 14/15 July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose office? I didn't quite understand this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you remember me showing you that log entry in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember. I saw this in Banja Luka, too, and I said that I, myself -- I mean, I thought it was probably that is what it was about. And then there's this date and then the police being engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees -- I mean, I said straight away that I personally took part in this, in this escort. And I don't know what else this could mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that reference on 14 July of engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees, you believe that's the escort you've just described to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go to 15 July in the logbook. Now, this says: "The police worked on searching and combing the area as well as apprehending the Muslims found hiding in the area." First of all, what area do you think they're talking about in this entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm in the sure. I think that this probably means that there was a possibility that during the night from those vehicles some people escaped and were still there in the territory of the town. I think that that is what this is about. I don't know what else it could mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Muslims were apprehended at some point on the 15th or 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear the interpretation now. I seem to be losing the volume all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How does it -- can you hear me okay now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you, but now I can hear the interpreter as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you become aware that Muslims had been apprehended on the 14th or 15th of July, as noted in this log entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know nothing about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next date, which says 17 July. Do you see the 17 July there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says: "The patrol worked at the checkpoints. Air raid sirens sounded at 4.00 a.m. Patrols worked on the apprehension and securing of Muslims in the municipal area of Bratunac and Srebrenica." What can you tell us about that, again the apprehension of Muslims from the Bratunac and Srebrenica areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then it goes on to say: "One police patrol remained in Pilica to secure and guard the Muslims." First of all, how much -- how many men are one police patrol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on how many were needed. If -- well, usually two people would be on a patrol. If it's a patrol, then it's two people. Two military policemen constitute one patrol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you order any Bratunac Brigade military policemen to secure prisoners in Pilica at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that I went to Zvornik and that at 10.00, around 10.00, perhaps even before that, I was positioned with a vehicle at this crossroads that I mentioned. I didn't know where I was going to. I didn't have any contact with them afterwards. I could not assign anyone to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you assign or order any Bratunac Brigade military policemen to go to Pilica on the 15th/16th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how they got up there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone steal your men without telling you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He's never indicated that anyone was stolen from him. He has indicated that Nikolic gives orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is pure obstruction, 100 per cent, Your Honour. He should stop. He should be told to stop this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm entitled to make a record. I'm entitled to object. And I'm entitled to some common courtesy by the Prosecution. And he should treat the witness with some courtesy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, maybe "steal" is not a proper word. You may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone take your men without your authorisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known who could have issued orders, and probably someone did issue them orders. Colonel Popovic could have returned and given them orders then. Momir Nikolic could have given them orders. Mladic could have given them orders. How can I say who gave them orders? How can I know who gave them orders when I did not even know they were there. I did not know who ordered them to do anything and no one informed me of everything. That's what I said in Banja Luka, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's someone else that could have given them orders, too, that you didn't mention, isn't there? Do you see that man in this room? Do you see that man today that could have issued orders to you to send people to Pilica? Do you see that man in the room today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have been given orders by my commander to send a patrol wherever necessary. However, I'm saying that no one ordered me to send that patrol and I did not send that patrol. Now, who did send the patrol is something I cannot say, because I was not in contact even with the police while I was there waiting for the column to be established. I did not even know why I had been positioned there and that I would be going anywhere, let alone me ordering someone to go to Pilica. I didn't even know where Pilica was. And I didn't know where I was going to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Did you get a report back from your military policemen about what was going on in Pilica on those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not a word?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the 15th of July, a bus load of Muslims pulled up to a school at Pilica and as the Muslim prisoners got off the bus, they were systematically shot? Did you hear that account from any Bratunac Brigade police officers that were securing Muslims at a school in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the form of the question. He hasn't established that those police officers that were there were there at the time that this atrocity occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think at the beginning of this trial, the Prosecution is instructed to ask some leading questions. I believe that this witness is not that friendly to the Prosecution, so this rule applies. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear -- did you get a report -- do you think that's funny? What do you think is funny about Muslims being butchered as they got off a bus? Is that what you're laughing at? Let me got to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he deserves an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm laughing because I hear here that someone said, I don't understand who, that my attitude towards the Prosecution is not friendly. If I did not have an attitude that was friendly to the Prosecution and to this Tribunal and if I was not respecting this Tribunal, I would not be here today. I would not be cooperating. I would not have been there in Banja Luka. So this offends me. This offends me and that's why I laughed. I mean, why are you saying that I'm not friendly to the Prosecution? I want the truth to be told and I want the truth to be proven. You cannot claim that I know something, that is, who gave the men the orders to do something when I was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, let me explain to you this term, "unfriendly." It is not in the ordinary sense. It is in the purely legal sense. Usually the word is used when there is a hostile witness, but in this situation I particularly avoid using that word because that will arouse other legal consequences. It's a purely legal terminology. It has nothing to do with your attitude in the courtroom, but it has something to do with your answers. I hope you could understand that. It is -- generally speaking, it is common law legal terms and it took me a long time to understand it. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour. But, Your Honour, what I see here, for example, when I smiled or laughed when this statement was made, the Prosecutor is trying to ascribe to me that I am laughing at the execution of the Muslims. This is provocative to my mind and I cannot stand it. It offends me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you have the right to explain the situation to us, and you have to believe that the Judges will be very impartial in this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, just to be clear, you were not laughing at the Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I laughed and I already said why, because you were proclaiming that I was an enemy of the Court, an enemy of the Prosecution, and I'm trying to help. Not only the Prosecution, not only the Court itself, but I'm trying to help the truth, because the Court, the International Tribunal was established in order to establish the truth, to find out what the truth was and in order to have justice done, to have justice carried out completely, not, for example, to condemn someone who is innocent and to let those who are guilty slip by, for instance. That is why I cannot understand that now I am the one who is an enemy of this Court, and I really want to cooperate. And I've been thinking so hard. I've been rewinding this tape in my head, so to speak, in order to remember these dates and events and everything, and if I'm to be blamed, then let me stay here straight away, no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, as the Judge explained to you, you're not the enemy of the Court, you're not the enemy of the Prosecution. You're no one's enemy. That was a purely legal term. I can tell the Court and I can tell you right now, you've always been friendly and very cooperative. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're trying to get to the truth. We've never had any problem, you and I, have we? You've always been cooperative and friendly to us, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep going through the questions. I know they're not easy and it's an emotional subject, so let's just keep going?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I tell you something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm supposed to ask you questions. You can talk to me afterward, of course. If you need to explain an answer --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wish to say now, please, because again you asked me whether I laughed at the execution of the Muslims from a bus. I did not laugh about that. I'm not a beast. I'm a man. I'm a person. I'm a human being who is gravely affected by everything that happened. I am not justifying the killing of one man. I'm not justifying the killing of an animal. Everyone has the right to live, let alone a bus load full of people. So I mean, you asked me whether I laughed about that. I cannot understand who would laugh about a thing like that. You would have been a monster in order to laugh about something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you think that the Bosnian Serb army systematically murdered all the men in that convoy you were leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this question, systematically and the entire army now. I mean, just I think it's sort of a global question. It's very broad. If he wants to tailor it, I don't have objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolute obstruction, Your Honour. It's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- army, systematically. That means that every single person in the VRS is guilty under their theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand your objection. It's -- really the question is too broad and systematically is a legal term. It's a legal term that will get the Witness confused. Well, to ease the tension, I think we might have a break. And we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have taken a deep breathe. We're ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let's go back to the logbook and just finish up a couple of entries, if we could. We were at the 17th. Let's just briefly go to the 18th. And the 18th it says: "The military police squadron worked according to plan." Do you know what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it worked on regular activities. I've already said what these regular activities are. It means that there weren't any special tasks involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next page. And you'll notice that there's no date on that next page, but if we go to the following page -- I'm sorry, go to the next page after the one with no date. And what date is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go back to the one with no date on it. So the one with no date on it, should that be the 19th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And it says: "During the shift, the police was engaged in notifying conscripts of their deployment." That's the usual task of the MPs, I take it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then it says: "No incidents." Then it says: "Patrols went to secure public utility workers in Glogova." Do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that -- it says here: "The patrol went to secure public utility workers in Glogova." That means that the patrol provided security for some workers of the public utilities that were doing something in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, on the 19th were you aware of what work was being secured by the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They were securing these workers who were doing something. Now, what these workers were doing, I don't know. I know that the patrol was securing these workers. Now, what they were doing, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th or before, were you aware of a large mass grave in the area of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not know at all that there was a mass grave there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And going briefly back to the Muslim men in the schools in Bratunac, did you see to it that those prisoners got sufficient water and food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see that. I do not know whether they got water and food, but it would be logical that they were receiving that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it the military's responsibility to see to it that prisoners in their custody get sufficient water and food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should not be the concern of the soldiers. It -- it's not that the soldiers had any resources. Somebody probably had to make sure that they had adequate provisions, that they had water and food, because they were on that assignment. But it is only natural that these people who were detained there in these facilities should receive food and water. Now, who was supposed to provide for this, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it, among others, Commander Blagojevic's responsibility to see that the prisoners in his custody --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. He's never stated that the prisoners were in his custody, Your Honour. There's no foundation and I think we're going way off base. If he wants to lay a foundation that those prisoners belong to the Bratunac Brigade, that those prisoners were Colonel Blagojevic's responsibility, that's fine, but no foundation has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but anyway those prisoners were in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Bratunac town. That doesn't make them Bratunac Brigade prisoners, Your Honour. And nothing has been established to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could briefly respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The record has established for various witnesses that the Bratunac Brigade was involved in Potocari in the separation and detention of the men. Momir Nikolic testified about that. And that they were transferred to Bratunac. We have now heard evidence that this individual and others were involved in the process of bringing prisoners that were coming in from the woods on the 13th of July and that they were transferred to Bratunac. Mostly, from this very witness, he has stated to Bratunac Brigade policemen were guarding these men at these schools in Bratunac. This is very close to the Bratunac headquarters. These prisoners are being guarded by Bratunac Brigade military policemen. That certainly is a foundation that Mr. Blagojevic has a responsibility over these prisoners. I understand Mr. Karnavas's defence, but objecting during cross-examination really isn't the time for him to be arguing his defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. The witness has also indicated that downtown Bratunac in the Hotel Fontana it was the forward command post for the Main Staff where Mladic, the head of the military, was there, as well as the Drina Corps where General Krstic was. And I think asking this witness or insinuating that the prisoners were the domain of the Bratunac Brigade I think is way off base. Now, if he wants to establish a foundation that those prisoners belonged to the Bratunac Brigade, that's another story. But so far all he's indicated was that he was told by Nikolic to provide some men to secure the prisoners, not that all those prisoners belonged. Where did Nikolic get that order? We don't know. But we do know that Popovic was giving orders, that Beara was giving orders, that Mladic was giving orders. But we haven't heard anything to the effect that the people that were in Bratunac town on those particular days belonged to the Bratunac Brigade. I don't believe that this witness is competent to answer that question. I know the Prosecution's theory, but he's not competent to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Whether the witness is competent to answer this question or not depends on what kind of answer the witness is going to offer us. I believe that there is sufficient basis for the Prosecution to ask this question. Witness, you may answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who was supposed to secure the supplies for the prisoners' water and food. Whether the military authorities were in charge, the corps command, the Main Staff or the civilian authorities. I really don't know whose duty it was or who was in a position to get those supplies for them. I know that I was in no position to do so. It wasn't within my power and it wasn't in my assignment. Probably someone was supposed to secure those, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is why I object to these sorts of talking objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a brigade commander generally responsible for the care of prisoners in his custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they are in his custody to begin with. I told you in Banja Luka that the whole operation that had been prepared. I wasn't even aware that the operation was being prepared. I thought it was a protected zone, that it was the Srebrenica enclave. The whole operation was run by the Main Staff. I don't know who gave the orders. I don't know who was in charge of what. Probably those top officers, top brass from the Main Staff knew that, the officers from the corps, top level. I can't talk about something that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you generally, a general question. Is a brigade commander responsible for prisoners in his custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who took them into custody to begin with. I don't know who brought them there. Therefore, I can't say who was responsible. I'm not here to judge. I am a witness before this Court. I can't determine the degree of responsibility of the different people involved. I am not familiar with the structure of the chain of command in the army. I'm just not familiar with that. I did not do my military service with the JNA, by virtue of having completed a three-year school, as I said, and on the basis of the law, it was prescribed that any student who completes his regular schooling in three years wearing uniform was not bound to do regular military service. Therefore, I was not even then familiar with the structure of command within the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were -- if the military police had captured Muslim prisoners, would you have been responsible for their care while they were in your custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If they were staying in the military police premises. If we had had an adequate gaol or premises to keep those people detained, in that case of course it would have been my responsibility to provide food for those people, just like members of the Dutch Battalion were given breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Those that the military police was providing security for, those staying in the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the military police were providing security for Muslims in those schools. Was anything provided to those Muslims in the way of care, food, water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anything was provided and whether it was possible to provide anything. I don't know if those people were given anything. It wasn't only the military policemen who were providing security there. There were large numbers of people there, so of course someone was supposed to provide as much food and water as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it your responsibility to see to it that the Muslims that your men are guarding are provided food and water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to do that. It wasn't my duty. I said there were large numbers of people there, and I was the lowest ranking person in that whole structure. It wasn't for me to decide. There was supposed to be a larger scale -- a large-scale involvement related to an activity like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did somebody above you decide that these men wouldn't get any food or water?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. It calls for speculation. And there's no foundation that this witness knows about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Pure obstruction objection again, Your Honour. It's an absolutely fair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would direct the Court to the question itself the way it's phrased. It's just an unfair question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's in response to his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, I hope you could put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what in the -- what is wrong with this question? Can you tell me? I don't see a thing wrong with this question. I don't want to argue with the Court, but what is wrong with this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe it calls for the speculation of this witness. This witness, I think, has done his best to answer your question. He could not get --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is his first reference to this very important subject, but I'll go on, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was supposed to be -- were you aware of any of the Muslims in these schools being interrogated for intelligence information by anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of anyone interrogating anyone else. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of a reburial operation that occurred some weeks after the fall of Srebrenica where bodies were moved from one location to another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that. I'm not sure when that happened, but I know that bodies were moved, probably from Glogova. Military police secured the road between Bratunac and Srebrenica. And lorries were used to transport this. Now, I have no idea where they were taking that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were the -- what precisely was the military police's involvement in this operation to move the bodies from Glogova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police provided security along the road so there wouldn't be any -- the lorries wouldn't have to stop for anything. You could feel the stench, and the convoy was passing through the town on its way to Srebrenica. We wanted to make sure the whole thing ran smoothly and that was the assignment that the military police, a single patrol, I believe, had to carry out, in terms of securing the road to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who ordered those military police officers to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara was in charge of that. He ran the operation. I'm not sure if he was the one who ordered it or if it was Nikolic. I can't remember which of the two gave the order. But it was ordered that a patrol should be sent to provide security for that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ordered to do anything to pass on orders to your people, or did they go around you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't remember whether I was told to send a patrol or whether, perhaps, Nikolic personally ordered the patrol. I really can't remember. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did this operation of taking bodies from Glogova last? How many days roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly. A day or two perhaps. I don't know how long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the trucks carrying the bodies go right through the town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right through the town of Bratunac, yes, and continued on towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people in town know this was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably did. Those who were outside in the street could see it, could feel it. You could feel the stench. So probably people talked and told one another about what was happening. Many people probably knew that those bodies were being moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your unit take part in any investigation into abuses of Muslims on 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware that the military police was abusing anyone, was involved in abusing anyone. At the military police headquarters, we had a legal expert, a legal advisor, Zlatan Celanovic who was in charge of legal matters. The military police carried out no investigations, nor did anyone task us to carry out any investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any military investigations into allegations of abuse of Muslim prisoners during the time frame of 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th July by soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't aware of that. This was probably the responsibility of the legal section, the legal advisors, the chief of security of the Bratunac Brigade of the corps, chief of security of the Main Staff. It would have been their responsibility, I assume. But I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware of any such investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such investigations, no. I know that it was not allowed to do that, that you were not supposed to stop a detainee, a prisoner. Now, as to whether someone actually did this and there was an investigation into that later on, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Bratunac Brigade soldiers or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not stop a detainee, abuse a detainee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Bratunac Brigade soldiers or officers ever being punished by anyone for abusing Muslims from the period of 12th July, 13th, 14th, 15th, 16th July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could hardly wait for the war to finally be over. I could hardly wait to return my equipment to the military. I don't know about any further activities that were being carried out. I'm not familiar with that. I really don't know if anyone was eventually punished or called to account. I know that I was never called for anything until I received a summons to go to Banja Luka, which I responded to in a timely manner. I was trying to recollect all those events, all the names, the dates involved, the time frame. I was trying to recall whatever I could in order to assist this Court, and I will keep on assisting this Court as much as I can. It is a United Nations Tribunal, which is the highest authority possible, and its work is supposed to be carried out in an impeccable manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe I do have some, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may move to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
